statement: In people admitted to hospital after a tramadol overdose, seizures were common, consciousness was often reduced and breathing was depressed enough to lower blood oxygen in some, while serotonin toxicity was not seen in the one series that looked for it and few people died in hospital; how often each happened differed widely between settings, many people had taken other medicines too, and no study read measured the risk for a person who takes tramadol. At one Australian toxicology unit (Ryan & Isbister, 2015), 71 admissions (70 people, November 2000 to June 2013) followed more than 400 mg, which the authors give as the maximum daily dose (median reported amount 1,000 mg; amounts and drugs as reported by the patients and others, not confirmed by laboratory tests); 51 had also taken other medicines, among them benzodiazepines (16), SSRI (13) and SNRI (10) antidepressants and tricyclic antidepressants (3). Seizures occurred in 8 of the 71 (11 in 100; exact 95% CI 5 to 21, editors' calculation): in 2 of the 20 who took tramadol alone and 6 of the 51 who took other medicines too, close to the 8 and 14 in 100 of two earlier series of tramadol exposures the authors cite. The first seizure came 1.5 to 22.7 hours after the overdose (median 8.5): 6.5 to 22.7 hours after slow-release tablets against 1.5 to 11 hours after immediate-release ones (8 people). People who had seizures had reported larger amounts (median 2,100 against 1,000 mg; p = 0.018 in the text and 0.021 in the figure legend), and the two seizures after the smallest amounts came with a predisposing reason (benzodiazepine withdrawal; an earlier seizure); but with 8 seizures and self-reported amounts this shows no safe amount, 3 of the 16 admissions left out because the amount was unknown also had seizures, and the authors cite a Tehran study in which seizures were unrelated to the amount, most after 500 to 1,000 mg. Consciousness was reduced (Glasgow Coma Scale below 15) in 29 of 71 (41 in 100) and deeply reduced (below 9, coma) in 5: three after tricyclic antidepressants and two with depressed breathing that responded to naloxone. Respiratory depression with oxygen saturation below 94% occurred in 13 of 71 (18 in 100; 10 to 29, editors' calculation), within 2 hours of the overdose in 7 of the 9 with a known time (5 and 8 hours in the other 2), in people who had reported larger amounts (median 2,500 against 1,000 mg; p = 0.003); 5 of the 13 had also taken a tricyclic antidepressant or promethazine or had pneumonia, and coma and respiratory depression are not reported separately for the 20 who took tramadol alone, although the authors say respiratory depression occurred with tramadol alone. A fast heart rate (no threshold stated) occurred in 27 (38 in 100), systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg in 32 (45 in 100), and vomiting or nausea in 36 (51 in 100). Naloxone, given in hospital to 9 people, improved oxygen levels or consciousness in 6, partly in 2 and not in 1, and no seizure was reported after it. Eight people, all of whom had taken other medicines, went to intensive care (5 for the other medicines' effects, 3 for breathing), and nobody died. No admission met the Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity, including people who had also taken SSRIs or SNRIs; one person who had also taken an escitalopram overdose had one of its signs (eye clonus) without meeting the criteria. None in 71 rules out only frequencies above about 5 in 100 in such overdoses (exact 95% upper limit 5.1 in 100, editors' calculation) and says nothing about tramadol at ordinary amounts or taken with antidepressants over time: the reports of serotonin toxicity the authors cite mostly involve tramadol taken with serotonergic antidepressants, and their conclusion about therapeutic doses goes beyond their data (reactions reported with MAOI antidepressants are covered in the answer on opioid painkillers taken with MAOIs). In Iran, a systematic review pooled hospital and poison-centre series of people admitted with tramadol poisoning, mostly young men, with a suicide attempt the commonest reason in most series that reported one and tramadol taken alone by 43 to 100 in 100 where this was reported (Rostam-Abadi et al., 2020): seizures were recorded in a pooled 34.6 in 100 (95% CI 29.6 to 39.8; 23 series, 5,972 admissions by the editors' sum; I² 94%), from about 12 to 69 in 100 in single series, with a prediction interval, the range in which a new series would be expected to fall, of 12.5 to 60.9 (read from the forest plot). Deaths in hospital were a pooled 0.7 in 100, or 7 in 1,000 (95% CI 0.0 to 1.9 in 100; 18 series, 4,761 admissions by the editors' sum; I² 92%; prediction interval 0 to 10.0 in 100): six series had none, and one series of 1,023 people in Kermanshah had 10 in 100, against 0.9 in 100 in a series of 546 from the same city and overlapping years. Breathing was reported unevenly: apnoea was among the three commonest other features listed for four series (3.6 to 6.2 in 100 in three, and 15.0 in 100 in a series of 20 children) and slowed breathing (18 in 100) for one, and changes in consciousness were among the commonest features. In four Iranian emergency departments and hospitals, tramadol poisoning was recorded in 22 in 100 first seizures (383 people), 37 in 100 of all seizures (141) and 40 and 55 in 100 of drug-induced seizures (143 and 137). The Iranian seizure figures are about three times the Australian one: the Australian authors suggest that some Tehran series drew patients selected for seizures, and the review's authors suggest that many people in Iran convert tramadol fast through a liver enzyme (CYP2D6), which no included study measured. The review found no study of poisoning or death among people who use tramadol; it was not preregistered and its authors call it exploratory; whether tramadol was confirmed by laboratory tests was not extracted; several series come from the same cities and periods and may count the same patients; and its pooled figures mix tramadol-only and mixed poisonings. Seizures at ordinary amounts were not measured in these papers and appear only in reports: in Iran's national reports of reactions blamed on tramadol (249 people, 2006–2010, 22.8 in 100 of the reports classed as prescribed use), seizure was the reaction most often reported (29.3 in 100 in the text, 29.5 in its table), and one case report describes a seizure after 200 mg by mouth with no other drug. Some people feel little from an amount of tramadol, and some then take more: the papers say, citing other work, that tramadol works largely through a breakdown product (O-desmethyltramadol) made by CYP2D6, whose activity differs between people with their genes and other medicines, and in the Australian series people who had seizures or low oxygen had reported larger amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can tramadol cause seizures, and what happens in an overdose? Seizures are common after a tramadol overdose. At one Australian hospital unit, 8 of 71 people treated after an overdose had seizures, as often after tramadol alone as with other medicines, some of them almost a day later. 18 in 100 had breathing trouble with low oxygen, 41 in 100 were less alert than normal and 5 went into a coma, 3 of them after also taking an older type of antidepressant. People who said they had taken more had more seizures and breathing trouble, and nobody died. No one met the criteria for serotonin syndrome, but with 71 people that rules out only rates above about 5 in 100 in such overdoses, and it says nothing about ordinary doses; earlier reported cases mostly involved tramadol taken with antidepressants. In Iranian hospitals, about 35 in 100 people treated for tramadol poisoning had seizures, with single studies ranging from 12 to 69 in 100, and about 7 in 1,000 died, though one study had 100 in 1,000. Many people had taken other medicines too, the amounts were not checked by lab tests, and nobody measured the risk for people taking tramadol at ordinary doses, where seizures appear only in reports. Some people feel little from an amount of tramadol and take more: its effect depends partly on a liver enzyme that works at different speeds in different people.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 24) and 6th paragraph (starting p. 24, continuing p. 25); Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 25)
evidence.extracted: The authors write, citing other work, that tramadol relieves pain mainly through its breakdown product O-desmethyltramadol, made by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, whose activity varies with other medicines and with genes (poor, intermediate and ultra-rapid metabolizers), and suggest, citing one Iranian study, that a high share of ultra-rapid metabolizers may partly explain Iran's high rates of poisoning, seizures and deaths; the review reports no metabolizer data from its included studies. They summarize seizures as almost 35% and deaths as 0.7% of admitted tramadol poisonings. Stated limitations include no longitudinal study of health outcomes in people using tramadol and, in some toxicological and forensic studies, no definite confirmation that tramadol was the only or main substance.

risk_of_bias.note: Australian series (card sc_ryan_2015: JBI, moderate): every admission to one unit, recorded prospectively by staff blinded to this study, but amounts and drugs were taken from patients' and others' accounts without laboratory confirmation, 41 of 112 admissions were left out (16 for an unknown amount, 3 of whom had seizures), tachycardia and the way seizures were ascertained are not defined, and nothing is adjusted for the other medicines most people took. Iranian review (card sc_rostam_abadi_2020: AMSTAR 2, critically low): no protocol, publication bias not considered, risk of bias not carried into the interpretation; the primary series were not appraised for laboratory confirmation, some may share patients, and some may have drawn patients selected for seizures. These problems could change the frequencies materially.

inconsistency.note: Seizures in 11 in 100 Australian admissions (and 8 and 14 in two earlier series the authors cite) against a pooled 34.6 in Iranian series that themselves range from about 12 to 69 in 100 (I² 94%; prediction interval 12.5 to 60.9); deaths from 0 to 10 in 100 between Iranian series (I² 92%), two from the same city and years giving 10 and 0.9. The suggested reasons (selection in Tehran, enzyme differences in Iran) were not tested. The statement gives the ranges, but no single frequency can be given with confidence.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the claim describes people admitted to hospital after an overdose and says that it gives no risk for people taking tramadol, for people who did not reach hospital or for ordinary amounts; the bound on serotonin toxicity is stated for such overdoses only.

imprecision.note: The Australian frequencies rest on few events (8 seizures and 13 people with respiratory depression; exact 95% intervals 5 to 21 and 10 to 29 in 100) and serotonin toxicity on none in 71 (upper limit 5.1 in 100), all given in the statement; the spread of the Iranian figures is counted under inconsistency. Not downgraded again.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; series of hospital admissions are reported whatever their frequencies, which do not depend on a significant result.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (frequencies among hospital admissions after a tramadol overdose): starts low; down one level for risk of bias and one for inconsistency; very low; never upgraded (descriptive claims are not). Status replicated: seizures in a substantial share of admissions were found independently in the Australian series and in the Iranian series (counted once, as one review), in the same direction but at very different frequencies. The figures for consciousness, respiratory depression, naloxone and the absence of serotonin toxicity rest on the Australian series alone (single study); the Iranian breathing data are listed for only five series, as one of each series' three commonest other features. The pooled Iranian death figure (0.7 in 100) gives the series similar weights; most of the deaths in the pooled series come from one series of 1,023 with 10 in 100 (editors' approximation from Figure 6). Seizures at ordinary amounts were not measured in any study read: the adverse-reaction reports and the case report show only that such seizures were reported. The sentence on feeling little rests on background statements both papers cite, not on their own measurements.

verification.flag_note: Question 17 of round pdf-2026-11-26 (forums theme 'Tramadol: effects and risks'). Not read: the series the Australian authors cite for 8 and 14 in 100 (Spiller et al., 1997, J Toxicol Clin Toxicol 35, 361–364; Marquardt et al., 2005, Ann Pharmacother 39, 1039–1044), the Tehran series (Shadnia et al., 2008; Talaie et al., 2009), the case reports of serotonin toxicity with antidepressants, and the two studies of seizures at prescribed doses in Ryan & Isbister's reference list (Gasse et al., 2000, Pharmacotherapy 20, 629–634; Gardner et al., 2000, Pharmacotherapy 20, 1423–1431), which would answer the part about ordinary doses; no DOIs printed. The review's supplements (Data S1–S5) are not on file. Iranian death-record shares (a pooled 5.7%, prediction interval 0 to 72.3%) are left out: they answer a different question and rest largely on unpublished data. Naloxone's response is given as a hospital finding in the statement only.
